questions.q: An ASML NXT:2100i (193.4 nm, NA 1.35) is run at a production k1 of 0.28. What is the approximate single-exposure half-pitch, and what happens to it at the theoretical k1 floor?
options: ~20 nm; at k1 = 0.25 it reaches ~10 nm, which is why SAQP was abandoned
~134 nm, because the effective wavelength in water is 193/1.44
~40 nm (80 nm pitch); at k1 = 0.25 it reaches ~36 nm, so ~72–80 nm is the tightest pitch 193i can print in one exposure
~72 nm; the k1 floor is 0.5 because only the 0th and +1st diffraction orders can ever enter the lens
questions.explanation: CD = k1·λ/NA = 0.28 × 193.4 / 1.35 ≈ 40 nm half-pitch. Two-beam imaging with off-axis illumination allows k1 down to 0.25 (≈ 36 nm), which is why 193i single-exposure pitches bottom out around 76–80 nm and tighter pitches need multi-patterning.

questions.q: In a chemically amplified resist, why is the post-exposure bake (PEB) rather than the exposure itself the step that determines the final line width?
options: The PEB evaporates the casting solvent, which is what makes exposed resist soluble in TMAH

Exposure only converts PAG molecules into a sparse latent image of acid; during PEB each acid molecule catalytically cleaves hundreds to thousands of protecting groups (t-BOC or tertiary esters) and diffuses 5–20 nm, so PEB temperature, time, and delay set both the chemical gain and the edge blur
The PEB cross-links the novolac resin so it survives the plasma etch
The PEB is where the DNQ undergoes the Wolff rearrangement to form indene carboxylic acid
questions.explanation: In a CAR the photon creates only an acid; deprotection happens thermally during PEB with the acid regenerated after every reaction (gain ~10^2–10^3). Acid diffusion during PEB is also the main resolution/LER/sensitivity trade-off knob, which is why PEB is controlled to ~0.1 °C and the exposure-to-PEB delay to seconds.

questions.q: Why did water immersion at 193 nm win over the 157 nm F2 excimer as the path beyond dry ArF?
options: 157 nm needed CaF2 for every lens element (intrinsic birefringence, boule supply), had no workable pellicle, and needed fluorinated resists with poor etch resistance, while water (n = 1.44, absorbing well under 1% in a 1 mm film) raised the NA from 0.93 to 1.35 using existing lens materials, masks, and resists, giving a larger resolution gain than the 193→157 wavelength step
Water absorbs strongly at 157 nm, so immersion was only possible at 193 nm; the industry chose immersion because it made resists cheaper
The F2 laser could not reach 6 kHz repetition rate, limiting throughput below 100 wph
157 nm light is EUV and requires vacuum and reflective optics
questions.explanation: The 157 nm programs were killed ~2003 by materials problems (CaF2 birefringence, no pellicle, poor resists). Immersion raises NA = n·sin θ to 1.35 with water, an effective wavelength of 134 nm, using the fused-silica lenses, 6% MoSi masks, and CAR platforms already in place.

questions.q: In self-aligned double patterning (SADP), what physically sets the width of the final lines, and what is the main design consequence of the process?
options: The lithographic mandrel CD sets the line width; the consequence is that overlay between the two exposures adds ~3–5 nm of space variation
The developer normality (0.26 N TMAH) sets the line width; the consequence is that only positive-tone resists can be used
The etch trim sets the line width; the consequence is that pitch cannot be reduced below the mandrel pitch

The ALD spacer thickness deposited on the mandrel sidewalls sets the line width (controllable to < 0.5 nm); because each spacer wraps around its mandrel, every line is a closed loop and line-ends must be created with a separate cut mask, which restricts the layer to 1D gridded lines at one pitch
questions.explanation: SADP prints mandrels at the relaxed pitch, deposits a conformal ALD spacer, etches it back, and pulls the mandrel; the two spacers per mandrel halve the pitch (80 → 40 nm) with CD set by deposition. The loops and single-pitch constraint are why cut masks and restricted 1D layouts appear at 20 nm and below; LELE, not SADP, is the scheme whose spaces depend on overlay.

questions.q: Depth of focus scales as k2·λ/NA². For the NA 1.35 immersion lens with k2 ≈ 0.6, what is the approximate total DOF, and which fab practices follow directly from it?
options: ~600 nm; resist films can be 1–2 µm thick and wafer leveling is unimportant
~60–65 nm; resists are only ~80–120 nm thick, spin-on-carbon/SiARC tri-layers planarize topography, and the scanner maps wafer height field by field with a level sensor on the second TWINSCAN stage
~6 nm; this is why 193i can only be used on perfectly flat bare-silicon wafers
~134 nm; this equals the effective wavelength in water
questions.explanation: DOF = 0.6 × 193.4 / 1.35² ≈ 64 nm total (±32 nm), the entire budget for wafer flatness, topography, chuck particles, leveling, and lens field curvature. Thin resists, planarizing underlayers, and per-field leveling on the measurement stage are the consequences.

questions.q: Which statement about EUV versus DUV layer usage at TSMC N5/N3-class nodes and the litho tool market is correct?
options: EUV replaced all 193i layers at N5; ASML's DUV business has since collapsed to a few percent of revenue
N3 uses EUV for all ~80 layers, which is why the mask count fell for the first time

N5 uses ~14 EUV layers and N3 ~20–25 out of roughly 80 mask layers, each EUV layer replacing several 193i multi-patterning exposures, so the majority of layers remain 193i/KrF/i-line; ASML holds ~90% of the litho market with DUV still about half its system revenue and China a large DUV customer
Nikon and Canon together hold about half the ArF immersion market, with ASML's dominance limited to EUV
questions.explanation: EUV took the ~15–25 tightest layers (fins, gates, contacts, M1–M4, cuts) where SAQP/LELELE were prohibitively expensive; layers that print in one 193i pass stay on DUV because they are cheaper. N5 was the first TSMC node with fewer masks than its predecessor. ASML is ~90% of litho by revenue; Nikon and Canon are a few percent each.

questions.q: A layer is qualified at "8% exposure latitude at 80 nm depth of focus". What does that statement mean, and which errors consume the budget it describes?
options: The laser must deliver exactly 8% of its rated power and the lens must be refocused every 80 nm of scan travel; the budget is consumed by stage speed and reticle heating

The dose may vary by ±4% and the focus by ±40 nm, in any combination, with the printed CD staying within ±10% of target; dose-equivalent errors (laser ~±0.3%, slit uniformity ~±0.3%, resist-thickness swing ~±1%, PEB temperature ~±0.4 nm of CD via ~2 nm/°C, i.e. ~±0.4% dose-equivalent at ~1 nm per 1% dose) and focus errors (levelling ~±15 nm, wafer flatness and topography ~±20 nm, chuck ~±10 nm, lens heating ~±10 nm, ~±29 nm in quadrature against the ±32 nm half-range) each eat into it, and the layer is manufacturable only if what remains is positive
8% of dies fail at the wafer edge because the immersion hood leaves 80 nm of water behind; the budget is consumed by watermarks
The resist absorbs 8% of the light in an 80 nm film; the budget is consumed by photon shot noise
questions.explanation: The process window is read from a focus-exposure matrix and its Bossung plot: exposure latitude is the full dose range (here ±4%) and DOF the full focus range (here ±40 nm) over which CD stays within ±10% and sidewall angle stays in spec. Every source of dose and focus error, added in quadrature or worst-case, is subtracted from that rectangle, which is why resists are ~100 nm, underlayers planarize, backsides are rinsed and the level sensor maps every field.

questions.q: At a 30 mJ/cm² ArF dose, why is a line-edge roughness of ~3–5 nm 3σ described as a statistical floor rather than an engineering defect, and what does the RLS scaling say it would cost to halve it?
options: Because the 193 nm laser's 0.3 pm bandwidth produces a 3–5 nm chromatic blur; halving LER requires a 0.15 pm laser
Because the developer normality (0.26 N) sets a 3–5 nm dissolution front; halving LER needs a double puddle

Because 30 mJ/cm² is ~2.9 × 10¹⁶ photons/cm², of which a 100 nm film absorbs only ~10%, giving ~10¹⁹–10²⁰ acids/cm³, so a 20 × 20 × 100 nm line segment holds only ~400 acids and its count fluctuates by √400 ≈ 5% (shot noise); with LER² × dose × resolution³ ≈ constant, halving LER at fixed resolution costs ~4× the dose
Because the ALD spacer in SADP is only controllable to 0.5 nm; halving LER needs a thicker spacer
questions.explanation: Roughness is seeded by counting statistics: a 6.4 eV photon carries 1.03 × 10⁻¹⁸ J, so 30 mJ/cm² is ~2.9 × 10¹⁶ photons/cm²; after ~10% absorption and imperfect acid generation the film holds ~10¹⁹–10²⁰ acids/cm³, one per 2–5 nm cube, and a 4 × 10⁻¹⁷ cm³ line segment contains only ~400, fluctuating by √400 = 20 (~5%). The resolution/LER/sensitivity triangle then says smoother edges at the same resolution need quadratically more photons, which is the same trade-off that limits EUV throughput.
